say.en: Time up equals time down.
Take upwards as positive. The ball leaves with speed u, and gravity gives acceleration minus g all the way.
At the top the velocity is zero. That gives the maximum height and the time to come back.
Its v–t graph is one straight line of slope minus g, crossing zero at the top.
So for u equal to 20 metres per second the ball rises 20 metres.

heading.en: Gravity and falling: feather vs hammer

tagline.en: Why heavy and light things fall together — and what the air changes.

myth.en: Heavier objects fall faster than light ones.

truth.en: Without air, everything falls at the same rate. A feather is slow only because air pushes up on it.

say.en: The Earth pulls every object towards its centre. That pull is called gravity, and it's why things fall when you let go.
Drop a heavy bowling ball and a light apple at the same moment. Surprise: they hit the ground together!
A falling object keeps speeding up: every second it goes about 10 metres per second faster. That's why the gaps between these snapshots keep growing.
A feather falls slowly because the air pushes up on it. This push is called air resistance, and it matters most for light, spread-out things.
On the Moon there is no air. An astronaut dropped a hammer and a feather, and they landed at the very same moment!
A heavier object gets a bigger pull, but it is also harder to speed up. The two cancel out, so everything speeds up at the same rate as it falls. We call that rate g.

goal.en: Drop things side by side and find out what really decides which lands first.

task.en: Drop the bowling ball and the apple.

explain.en: They land together, even though the ball is 70 times heavier. Gravity speeds up heavy and light things at the same rate.

question.en: A 7 kg bowling ball and a 100 g apple are dropped together. Which lands first?

options.en: The bowling ball — heavier things fall faster

task.en: Drop the hammer and the feather.

explain.en: The feather drifts down slowly. Air pushes up on it as it falls — that push is called air resistance — and for a light, fluffy feather the push is big compared with its weight.

question.en: Now a hammer and a feather, in air. Which lands first?

task.en: Drop a paper ball and a flat sheet.

explain.en: Same weight, different shape. The flat sheet catches much more air, so air resistance slows it far more. It's the air, not the weight, that makes the difference.

question.en: Two sheets of the same paper (same weight). One is crumpled into a ball. Which lands first?

task.en: Take the air away and drop the hammer and feather.

explain.en: With no air there is no air resistance, so they land at exactly the same moment. An astronaut did this on the Moon in 1971.

question.en: With no air at all (a vacuum, like on the Moon), which lands first?

takeaway.en: Without air, everything falls at the same rate, however heavy; air resistance is what slows light, spread-out things.

caption.en: Leo is sure that heavy things fall faster than light things.
He drops the bowling ball and an apple from the treehouse. Thud! They land at the same moment.
Maya drops a feather. It drifts down slowly, because the air pushes up against it.

speech.en: Then why is the feather slow?

caption.en: She drops two identical sheets, one crumpled up. Same weight, but the crumpled one lands first: air makes the difference.

limits.en: “Everything falls at the same rate” is only true when air resistance is tiny. The value of g depends on where you are: it's about 1.6 m/s² on the Moon, and slightly less on a mountain top than at sea level. For very fast, very massive things, Einstein's relativity describes gravity better than pushes and pulls.

problem.en: A ball is thrown up at 20 m/s (g = 10 m/s²). Find the maximum height and the time to return.

narration.en: Let us solve this together. A ball is thrown up at 20 m/s (g = 10 m/s²). Find the maximum height and the time to return.

say.en: Let us solve this together. A ball is thrown up at 20 metres per second (g equals 10 metres per second squared). Find the maximum height and the time to return.
H equals u squared/2 grams equals 400 over 20 equals 20 metres.
T equals 2u/g equals 40 over 10 equals 4 seconds.
So the answer is 20 metres; 4 seconds.
